candidates.statement: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is issuing this guidance to assist industry 16 and State and local governments in understanding how to categorize the entities in the drug 17 supply chain in accordance with the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA). 2 This guidance 18 revises the Agency’s draft guidance for industry Identifying Trading Partners Under the Drug 19 Supply Chain Security Act (August 2017) to address the status of some entities as trading 20 partners (e.g., private-label distributors, salvagers, and returns processors and reverse logistics 21 providers), provide clarification on certain drug distribution scenarios, and address the 22 interpretation of section 582(a)(7) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 23 which discusses third-party logistics providers (3PL) licensure status prior to the effective date of 24 the forthcoming regulations establishing licensure standards. The DSCSA establishes product 25 tracing requirements for certain trading partners in the drug supply chain, including 26 manufacturers, repackagers, wholesale distributors, and dispensers. The DSCSA also requires 27 that trading partners of manufacturers, wholesale distributors, dispensers, and repackagers must 28 meet the applicable requirements for being “authorized trading partners.” 3 Additionally, the 29 DSCSA requires FDA to issue regulations that establish Federal standards for the licensing of 30 wholesale drug distributors 4 (WDDs) and 3PLs. The Agency is currently drafting these 31 regulations. This guidance, when finalized, will explain FDA’s current thinking on how certain 32

candidates.statement: Section 583 of the FD&C Act requires FDA to issue regulations regarding the standards for 153 licensure of wholesale distributors under section 503(e)(1) of the FD&C Act. Section 503(e) of 154 the FD&C Act establishes licensure requirements based on these standards and adds reporting 155 requirements for WDDs. Specifically, section 503(e)(1), subject to section 583 of the FD&C 156 Act, prohibits an entity from engaging in wholesale distribution of prescription drugs in any 157 State unless such entity is licensed by the State from which the drug is distributed, or by FDA if 158 such State from which the drug is distributed has not established a licensure requirement. 159 Furthermore, under certain circumstances, 12 such wholesale distributor must also be licensed by 160 the State into which the drug is distributed. Section 503(e)(2) of the FD&C Act requires WDDs 161

candidates.statement: FDA interprets this provision to mean that a 3PL is fully licensed for DSCSA purposes during 203 the period prior to the effective date of Federal 3PL licensure regulations (provided that the 3PL 204 utilizes good product handling and distribution practices), notwithstanding a situation where a 205 State requires licensure of the 3PL during this period and the 3PL does not hold such State 206 licensure. This interpretation should not be construed to impact the ability of States to require 207 licensure of 3PLs under State law or the validity of such State licensure. Rather, the Agency's 208 view reflects FDA’s understanding that in enacting section 582(a)(7) of the FD&C Act, Congress 209 intended 3PLs to be deemed licensed for DSCSA purposes to facilitate supply chain operations 210 until the Federal licensing standards take effect. 211
